<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - Gemmini is a hardware‐accelerator generator and full‐stack DNN evaluation platform built on the Chipyard ecosystem.  
   - It uses Chisel (Scala DSL) to describe a RoCC accelerator that plugs into a RISC-V Rocket or BOOM core tile, enabling exploration of systolic‐array designs, DMA engines, scratchpads, and custom instructions for DNN workloads.  

2. File Structure Analysis  
   - Top-level directories:  
     • `.github/` and CI scripts—deployment and testing workflows (Verilator, Spike).  
     • `modeling/`—static performance modeling (Timeloop integration).  
     • `scripts/`—build helpers for ONNX and training/inference images.  
     • `software/`—C libraries, test suites, ONNX-Runtime port, shell wrappers.  
     • `src/main/scala/gemmini/`—Chisel RTL modules (controllers, mesh, DMA, scratchpad, FIFO queues, TLB).  
     • `src/test/scala/gemmini/`—unit tests for RTL components.  
     • Build/config: `build.sbt`, `project/`, Scala style configs.  

3. Key Architectural Insights from README  
   - Gemmini is a decoupled access/execute accelerator with three controllers: ExecuteController (systolic array + transposer), LoadController (DMA in to scratchpad/accumulator), and StoreController (DMA out + optional max-pooling).  
   - Private memories: Scratchpad (inputType banks) and Accumulator (accType banks + adders/scalers/activations).  
   - Systolic array organized as MeshWithDelays → Tiles → PEs, supporting weight- or output-stationary dataflows.  
   - Custom ISA: `mvin`/`mvout`, `config_*`, `matmul.preload`/`compute`, and higher-level CISC loop instructions.  
   - Connectivity: Gemmini attaches via the Rocket Chip RoCC interface to the TileLink system bus, sharing the L2 cache and memory‐subsystem.  

4. How to Draw the System Design Diagram  
   a. Main Components  
      - Host CPU (Rocket/BOOM core)  
      - RoCC Accelerator Interface  
      - ExecuteController  
      - LoadController & StoreController  
      - Systolic Array (MeshWithDelays → Tiles → PEs)  
      - Transposer  
      - Scratchpad SRAM banks  
      - Accumulator SRAM banks + adders/scalers/activations  
      - DMA engines (read/write) + TLB/PTW  
      - System Bus (TileLink) → L2 cache → DRAM  
      - Software Stack (C library, ONNX-Runtime)  
      - Simulators (Spike, Verilator, FireSim)  
   b. Relationships & Data Flows  
      - Show directional arrows:  
        • Host CPU issues custom Gemmini instructions over RoCC → controllers.  
        • LoadController → DMA → Scratchpad/Accumulator.  
        • ExecuteController → Systolic Array → returns results to Scratchpad/Accumulator.  
        • StoreController → DMA → System Bus → DRAM.  
      - TLB/PTW shared with host CPU for virtual → physical address translation.  
      - MeshWithDelays inputs (A, B, D) and outputs (C) flow between scratchpad, systolic array, and accumulator.  
   c. Architectural Patterns & Principles  
      - Decoupled Access/Execute: separate pipelines for load, compute, and store.  
      - Scratchpad-based memory: explicit software‐managed local memories.  
      - Systolic array with two‐tier pipeline (Tiles + PEs).  
      - Parameterized generator: all components (array dimensions, types, queue lengths, dataflows) configured at elaboration time.  
      - CISC loop unrollers for transparent tiling and double‐buffering.  
   d. Technologies & Libraries  
      - Chisel (Scala) for RTL  
      - TileLink interconnect (Rocket Chip)  
      - RISC-V RoCC custom instructions  
      - ONNX-Runtime (software/onnxruntime-riscv)  
      - Simulators: Spike (functional), Verilator/VCS (cycle-accurate), FireSim (FPGA-accelerated)  

5. Tailoring Guidelines for a Hardware Accelerator Project  
   - Emphasize separation between host CPU, RoCC interface, and accelerator controllers.  
   - Illustrate internal modules (controllers, scratchpad, DMA, systolic array) as distinct boxes.  
   - Depict memory hierarchy: scratchpad/accumulator banks vs. shared L2/DRAM.  
   - Show configuration flow: parameters passed at generator/elaboration time vs. runtime ISA commands.  

6. Diagram Conventions  
   - Labels: use clear, descriptive names (e.g., “ExecuteController”, “Scratchpad Bank”).  
   - Arrows: show data-path directions (e.g., “mvin → DMA → Scratchpad”, “matmul → MeshWithDelays”).  
   - Color/Shading:  
     • One color for compute elements (controllers, PEs).  
     • Another for memory elements (SRAM banks, caches).  
     • A third for interconnect/bus.  
   - Shapes:  
     • Rectangles for modules, cylinders for memories.  
     • Dashed lines for control/config paths.  

7. Level of Detail  
   - Capture each of the three controllers and their interactions with shared resources.  
   - Show the two-tier hierarchy within the systolic array (Tiles → PEs).  
   - Include the TLB → PTW fallback path.  
   - Represent the CISC loop FSMs that double-buffer tiles.  
   - Don’t omit simulator interfaces—indicate how software and host interact with the accelerator.  

By structuring your diagram around these components, interactions, and conventions, you’ll produce a detailed, accurate, and project-specific system design diagram for Gemmini.  
</explanation>
